Hi Alice / Sanjay —

Thanks again for the 30m earlier — really helpful to see the flow and your performance constraints. Per our discussion I wanted to recap the SLOs you mentioned and call out a few follow-ups before we scope a short POC: 

Key SLOs you mentioned:
- Latency target: p95 <= 150ms for the user-visible generation step
- Sustained throughput: ~50 QPS (mixed small/large prompts)
- Concurrent sessions: ~8 active users per service instance (burst to 20)
- Streaming: required for perceived interactivity on long outputs
- Context window: up to 32k tokens (mostly 24k typical), output max tokens ~2k

A couple of notes that will affect inference design and latency:
1) Context window & tokenization: if your average prompt size is 10–15k tokens, the KV-cache and sequence processing will materially affect per-token latency and GPU memory footprint.
2) Max output size (2k tokens) + streaming: streaming reduces time-to-first-token but end-to-end completion time still scales with total output tokens. For p95 latency guarantees we should scope both time-to-first-byte and end-to-end generation windows.
3) Batching & concurrency trade-offs: to meet 50 QPS and p95 <=150ms we’ll likely need a combination of small-request batching and a reserved-pool configuration (Dedicated) to avoid noisy neighbors.

Next steps I propose:
- Can you confirm a small set of sample payloads (we chatted about three: short search prompt ~200 tokens, mid-length context ~6k tokens, long context ~18–24k tokens)? Attach if possible.
- Sanjay: do you require FULL streaming (chunked tokens to client) or would a hybrid (time-windowed flush) suffice for the first pass?
- Redwood can run a targeted load test (50 QPS mix) using your samples if you provide access or allow us to run against a staging endpoint. That will give realistic p95 numbers and tail behavior.

I've attached a rough SLA draft and a quick perf-report template we use for POCs. Looping in Vivek and Rishi to scope the engineering implementation and test plan.

Best,

Thanks for the context — a few engineering notes that will help set expectations for the POC: 

1) Context window impact: latency per token is roughly linear in sequence length for the attention/kv steps; a jump from 6k -> 18k tokens increases per-token processing overhead and KV cache management cost. Practically, expect 20–40% higher GPU time per token for the long prompts depending on model architecture and attention optimizations.

2) Streaming vs time-to-first-token: if you need time-to-first-byte < 50ms, we will prioritize a streaming-optimized path with lower internal batching and reserved capacity; this increases cost but reduces p95 tail.

3) Quantization & memory: 4-bit quantization will reduce memory but can increase pure compute latency slightly for some kernels. For a Dedicated POC we recommend using a 4-bit quantized variant to fit 32k context on a single GPU during tests, then measure latency impact.

4) Batching policy: to hit 50 QPS while maintaining p95 <=150ms, we’ll run continuous micro-batching with a max batch window of 5–10ms and a reserved pool sized for your concurrency pattern. We’ll include adaptive batching in the test harness.

Action items for Redwood (I can lead the POC SE work):
- Prepare server image with quantized model + streaming stack
- Run controlled load tests (short/mid/long mixes) and produce p50/p95/p99 token latency and time-to-first-byte metrics
- Provide expected GPU memory usage and recommended Dedicated instance size

I’ll draft a simple test plan and post it to the Drive link Marissa shared.

—Rishi
